newsitem.title: CHILE: NASA robot practices for Mars on Chilean desert.
newsitem.headline: NASA robot practices for Mars on Chilean desert.

text.p: A NASA robot the size of a small car began a lengthy trek this week across the Chilean desert to practice for missions on more distant landscapes -- like the moon and Mars.

The four-wheeled Nomad robot, developed by scientists at Carnegie-Mellon University in Pittsburgh, began a 124-mile (200 km) crawl across the Atacama desert on Wednesday that its creators hope will give them insight into how a similar machine would work on other planets.
The robot, like a dune buggy bristling with antennae and cameras, is a prototype of a machine that NASA plans eventually to send on unmanned spaceshots.
Unlike machines on past Mars missions, which gathered rocks and took pictures only in the immediate vicinity of their landing site, Nomad is designed to travel.

"The space missions we've had until now allowed us to gather information in small areas. With the Nomad, we can gather information from up to 200 kilometres (124 miles)," said Hans Thomas of NASA as he checked a hilltop antenna used to beam orders to the robot from the United States.

The landscape chosen by scientists near the oasis of San Pedro de Atacama is about as unearthly as you can get and still be on earth. The world's driest place, it has virtually no rainfall, no vegetation and very few people.

Part of the Nomad's trip will take it over the vast Atacama saltflats, the only remnant of the ocean that covered the area millions of years ago, and now surrounded by a stunning backdrop of fuming volcanos and snow-dusted peaks.
Apart from looking and feeling like another planet, the Atacama has other features that make it ideal for the trek, said scientists.

"It happens to be the driest desert in the world, it has a great variety of terrains -- and it's in the same time zone as the eastern United States," which puts less strain on the scientists who will send orders to Nomad by satellite, said Chilean scientist Alex Foessel, from Carnegie-Mellon.

Crawling at a speed of about two-thirds of a mile (one km) per hour, the robot will take about five weeks to make the trek across the Atacama while testing its antennae, cameras, machinery and steering with as little human intervention as possible.
"We'll be trying out technologies that...will allow the robot to take care of itself," said Foessel.
Information from the robot will take about 1.5 seconds to travel to controllers in Pittsburgh, compared to the 19 minutes it would need to send information to earth from Mars.
Because of that time lag, "the robot is going to need a certain capacity to direct itself in emergency situations," said U.S. scientist Eric Rollins.

The robot is very similar but not identical to the one which would be used on the moon or other planets. The main difference, scientists said, is that Nomad is powered by gasoline and those on Mars or the moon would be nuclear or solar-powered.
